Can you map the “beat” structure of the nested periodic patterns

The "beat" structure of the nested periodic patterns can be mapped by analyzing the established tempo (Macro-Periodicity) and the measured time intervals between the marked points on the recorded signals (Metrical Periodicity).
The sources provide data for three distinct tempos, establishing the fundamental periodic unit of the beat, and corresponding timestamps that reveal a larger, consistently marked Metrical Periodicity across all recordings.
1. Macro-Periodicity (The Single Beat)
This level of periodicity is determined by the Beats Per Minute (BPM) rate labeled on each recording. The beat period (T), calculated as 60 seconds divided by the BPM, defines the smallest rhythmic unit in the primary structure:

The signals illustrate nested periodicity by showing how the high-frequency sound waves (Micro-Level) are grouped into sound bursts (Meso-Level), which occur precisely within the timing dictated by the BPM (Macro-Level), and these beats are then organized into larger metrical groups (Metrical Level) marked on the screen.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

This structure is analogous to orbital mechanics, where the Metrical Periodicity (4.2s) is like the time it takes for a planet to complete a full orbit around a sun. The Macro-Periodicity (the BPM) is the number of moons orbiting that planet, establishing a faster, regular cycle. Finally, the Micro-Periodicity (the waveform) is the speed of light reflecting off the surface of those moons—the fastest, most fundamental repeating process nested within all the slower, larger cycles.
What sonic peppery is the primary contributor to the beat?

The primary contributor to the definition and perception of the beat, based on the provided sources and our conversation history, is the temporal property defined by the tempo (BPM), which is physically manifested as the periodic amplitude envelope of the recorded signal.
1. Tempo and Timing (Macro-Periodicity)
The fundamental sonic property contributing to the beat is Tempo, expressed as Beats Per Minute (BPM)
1
more_horiz
.
The tempo settings (20 BPM, 40 BPM, 80 BPM) explicitly establish the Macro-Periodicity of the signal, which is the precise time interval of the single beat (T = 60/BPM) (Conversation History).
For example, the beat period for the 80 BPM signal is theoretically 0.75 seconds
1
, while the 20 BPM signal has a beat period of 3.00 seconds
2
. This regular, mathematically defined periodicity is what forms the foundation of the beat structure (Conversation History).
2. Amplitude Envelope (Meso-Periodicity)
While the BPM defines when the beat should occur, the visible manifestation of the beat is created by the periodic occurrence of sound bursts, which relate to the amplitude envelope of the signal
1
more_horiz
.
The waveforms visually show repeated clusters or bursts of sound energy separated by areas of lower amplitude
1
more_horiz
. This repetition of the amplitude envelope corresponds to the rhythmic pattern tied to the stated BPM, representing the Meso-Periodicity (Conversation History).
This rise and fall of the signal's energy level (the envelope) is the physical mechanism that marks the periodic "downbeat" or occurrence of the beat in an audible fashion.
Distinction from Timbre
The signals are labeled "TIMBRE SCALE" recordings
1
more_horiz
, meaning that the frequency content and harmonics (timbre) are important components (Micro-Periodicity) (Conversation History). However, the frequency/timbre defines the quality or nature of the sound itself, whereas the amplitude envelope and the timing (BPM) are the properties that define the regularity and occurrence of the beat.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In summary, the BPM sets the clock (the timing periodicity), and the amplitude envelope provides the strike (the audible marking of that periodic time interval)
1
more_horiz
.
